title: Adiabatic training of VQAs for entanglement detection
authors: E. Acosta, C. Cano, D. Manzano, G. Botella
abstract: This paper introduces a hybrid quantum framework for training Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) aimed at addressing the fundamental problem of entanglement detection using adiabatic quantum computing. This problem is of foundational significance in quantum information science and has been approached through both classical and quantum methodologies. We propose an adiabatic-inspired optimization strategy for training VQAs, which combines a discretization of the parameter space with a hierarchical segmentation scheme. The optimization problem is formulated as a Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization (QUBO) model to leverage the capabilities of quantum annealing. Preliminary results are compared against classical neural networks and conventional VQA training techniques. The findings aim to stimulate further investigation and discussion within the scientific community regarding the efficacy and applicability of the proposed approach.

infographic.key_insight: An adiabatic-inspired approach trains variational quantum algorithms for entanglement detection by encoding parameter optimization as a QUBO problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to using quantum annealing for VQA training, with parameter discretization and hierarchical segmentation shaping implementation.

Apply a hierarchical segmentation scheme.
Formulate training as Quadratic Unconstrained Binary Optimization for quantum annealing.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports preliminary comparisons with classical neural networks and conventional VQA training, but provides no datasets, metrics, or quantitative outcomes.
infographic.watch_item: QUBO size and discretization accuracy may limit scalability; practical advantages remain unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Adiabatic training of VQAs for entanglement detection

title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes
authors: Hong-Ye Hu, Zhenlai Wang, Binzhao Luo, Tao Xiang, Chen Zhao
abstract: Quantum error correction is essential for fault-tolerant quantum computing. High-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes have emerged as a promising approach to reducing the substantial physical qubit overhead of quantum error correction, enabling encoding rates exceeding $1/2$ in blocks of approximately one thousand physical data qubits. However, their practical implementation requires decoders that combine high accuracy with low latency to keep pace with quantum hardware. Existing decoders of high-rate qLDPC codes can achieve high accuracy but often incur substantial computational latency, whereas neural network decoders have yet to be demonstrated for high-rate qLDPC codes. Here, we introduce \emph{neural triage decoding}, a framework that uses syndrome consistency to adaptively allocate neural computation. A local neural message-passing network rapidly predicts error corrections, additional iterations reduce residual syndrome violations, and a rarely invoked diversification stage searches for consistent corrections to the remaining shots. We demonstrate that the \texttt{Triage} decoder can decode ultra-high-rate qLDPC codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, including lifted-product and Kasai codes, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy comparable to the near optimal algorithmic decoders while reducing decoding latency by approximately one to two orders of magnitude. Our framework is inspired by a rigorous analysis of the exact bitwise marginal decoder, revealing a distance-independent syndrome-inconsistent error floor. In addition, we show the robustness of neural network decoders to mismatched error priors. Our results establish adaptive neural decoding as a promising route towards fast, accurate, and scalable quantum error correction in the near term.

infographic.key_insight: Neural triage decoding adaptively spends computation on difficult error patterns, achieving high accuracy with substantially lower latency for ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Faster decoding of high-rate codes could help reduce physical-qubit overhead while keeping quantum error correction responsive to hardware timing constraints.
method: Use a local neural message-passing network to rapidly predict error corrections.
Add iterations when corrections leave residual syndrome violations.

infographic.evidence_signal: On lifted-product and Kasai codes encoding a few hundred logical qubits, the abstract reports accuracy comparable to near-optimal algorithmic decoders with approximately 10–100× lower decoding latency.
infographic.watch_item: Real-time deployment requires checking tail latency, since difficult cases trigger extra iterations and diversification.
infographic.paper_title: Fast and accurate neural triage decoding of ultra-high-rate quantum LDPC codes

title: Digital-Analog Quantum Neural Network with Long-Range Interactions
authors: Zongyuan Ge, Daili Li, Zewen Zhang
abstract: Protocols combining single-qubit digital operations with analog quantum evolutions bypass large numbers of two-qubit entangling gates, offering a promising approach to variational algorithms and hybrid quantum simulation. Focusing on the digital-analog quantum neural network (DA-QNN) as a representative framework, this work demonstrates that incorporating long-range interactions enhances the efficiency of such hybrid algorithms. Within the analog blocks, an Ising model with power-law interactions is employed to generate entanglement, and this protocol is benchmarked across supervised and unsupervised learning tasks. Beyond discussing the effects of the transverse field and evolution time, the primary analysis focuses on how the interaction range governs the expressibility and trainability of the ansatz. For supervised image classification and many-body phase detection, long-range ansatzes match the performance of their short-range counterparts with fewer DA-QNN layers or shorter evolution times, owing to the rapid information propagation across the system enabled by nonlocal couplings. This resource reduction alleviates the classical optimization overhead and eases experimental implementation. In unsupervised phase detection, although the long-range ansatz does not outperform its short-range counterpart in every regime, the two ansatzes provide complementary signatures that jointly reconstruct the complete phase diagram. These findings establish long-range interacting platforms as a compelling resource for advancing practical, large-scale digital-analog quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: Long-range interactions let digital-analog quantum neural networks match short-range models on supervised tasks with fewer layers or shorter evolution times.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining single-qubit gates with long-range analog entanglement can reduce circuit resources and classical optimization overhead, potentially easing experimental implementation.

title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning
authors: Liangnuo Zhang, Tanner Culpitt, Qiwei Yin, Linghua Zhu, Xiaosong Li
abstract: Data encoding is a central challenge in quantum machine learning (QML), as it determines how classical information is mapped onto quantum states and influences the expressive power and efficiency of parameterized quantum circuits. Here, we introduce a physics-informed quantum encoding strategy that exploits the intrinsic many-body structure of electronic systems to establish a direct correspondence between the body order of input descriptors and the locality of quantum gates. Specifically, $n$-body electronic descriptors obtained from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation are encoded through $n$-qubit gates, yielding a systematic hierarchy of quantum circuits with increasing many-body expressivity. Using reduced-density-matrix descriptors, we construct quantum machine-learning models incorporating one- through four-body encodings and benchmark their performance in predicting electron-correlation energies along bond-stretching potential energy surfaces. We demonstrate that increasing the body order of the encoding systematically improves prediction accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit. Remarkably, disconnected many-particle densities constructed from lower-order electronic information achieve accuracy comparable to explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases, providing a computationally inexpensive route to higher-body quantum encodings. These findings establish a connection between the many-body structure of classical data and the design of quantum feature maps, offering a systematic, physically interpretable framework for enhancing the expressivity and predictive performance of quantum machine-learning circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Matching electronic descriptor body order to quantum-gate locality creates a physically interpretable encoding hierarchy that improves quantum machine-learning predictions of electron-correlation energies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach guides quantum feature-map design using mean-field electronic data, with lower-order information offering an inexpensive route to higher-body encodings.
method: Extract electronic descriptors from a single mean-field electronic-structure calculation.
Map n-body descriptors to n-qubit gates, constructing one- through four-body encodings.
Compare reduced-density-matrix encodings, including disconnected many-particle densities built from lower-order information.
infographic.evidence_signal: On bond-stretching potential energy surfaces, higher-body encodings systematically improved accuracy toward the full configuration interaction limit, while disconnected densities matched explicitly correlated two-particle densities in key cases.

infographic.paper_title: Electronic-Structure-Informed Many-Body Encoding for Quantum Machine Learning

title: Hybrid Quantum Algorithms for Trade Surveillance Analytics
authors: Bimal Mehta, Daniel musgrove, Devanshu Shekhar, Shiplu Sarkar, Vanshaj Kerni, Varun Puram
abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) and trade surveillance remain largely manual: rule-based monitoring raises alerts of which, by estimate, over 95% are false positives, each reviewed by a human analyst. We benchmark four quantum and hybrid classifiers against classical baselines on a synthetic pump-and-dump detection task: a fidelity-based quantum k-nearest-neighbours classifier (QKNN) with clustering-based routing; a quantum support vector machine (QSVM) on a one-body projected quantum kernel; a 20-qubit quantum neural network (QNN) with a Pauli-ZZ feature map and RealAmplitudes ansatz; and a hybrid quantum neural network (HQNN) in which a small classical network generates every rotation angle of a five-qubit circuit. Baselines are logistic regression, XGBoost, one- and three-hidden-layer neural networks, and classical k-nearest neighbours. All models share one stratified split of 1000 accounts (800 train, 200 test, 20% suspicious) and two 20-feature representations (ANOVA and PCA); QKNN and QSVM are also tested under simulated noise, and the HQNN is run on the ibm_fez processor. The best model is classical XGBoost on ANOVA features, at a suspicious-class F1 of 61.4%. The HQNN is the strongest quantum-hybrid model, at 54.5-57.9% F1 on an ideal simulator and 55.4-59.8% on ibm_fez, ahead of six of eight classical configurations; at a 15% false-positive rate, half its alerts are genuinely suspicious. Versus the QNN (42.0% F1), it raises under half the false alarms at similar recall with a quarter of the qubits. The QKNN reaches 43.5% F1 (44.4% under noise), above classical KNN (35.6%); the QSVM does not exceed 41%. We observe no quantum advantage, but a five-qubit hybrid on today's noisy hardware already matches well-tuned classical models, with room to grow via richer circuits and larger devices. We contribute a like-for-like comparison with classical models on shared data, splits and features.

infographic.key_insight: A five-qubit hybrid quantum neural network achieved 55.4–59.8% suspicious-class F1 on IBM hardware, but classical XGBoost remained best at 61.4%.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact hybrid circuits merit further benchmarking for trade surveillance, though these results do not establish quantum advantage or production readiness.

infographic.paper_title: Hybrid Quantum Algorithms for Trade Surveillance Analytics

title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks
authors: Vincent Gurgul, David Prinz
abstract: Quantum Neural Networks (QNNs) offer a framework for learning functions from classical data, but their expressive power depends critically on how inputs are encoded into quantum states. Angle encoding can require resources that scale with the number of features, whereas amplitude encoding represents $d$ features using only $\mathcal{O}(\log_2 d)$ qubits. This compactness comes at a representational cost: normalization makes conventional amplitude encoding invariant to nonzero real rescaling of the input, up to an unobservable global phase. We show that this invariance induces an exact, architecture-independent restriction on the resulting hypothesis class. No downstream quantum circuit can distinguish inputs differing by nonzero real scaling. We develop a general condition under which deterministic preprocessing can remove this ambiguity and show that nonlinearity alone is insufficient. Based on this analysis, we introduce a fixed nonlinear feature map that provably distinguishes all real inputs under subsequent amplitude encoding, without adding trainable parameters and while retaining logarithmic qubit scaling. We evaluate the resulting QNN on three canonical classification benchmarks and a nonlinear synthetic dataset against conventional amplitude and angle encoding, as well as a classical neural network. Across these tasks, the proposed encoding consistently improves classification accuracy over both quantum encoding baselines by 21$-$44 %. Our results establish normalization-induced scale invariance as a concrete representational bottleneck of amplitude encoding and demonstrate that it can be removed while preserving a compact quantum representation, marking a step toward quantum models capable of capturing arbitrary relationships in classical data.

infographic.key_insight: Conventional amplitude encoding makes nonzero real-scaled inputs indistinguishable, but a fixed nonlinear feature map removes this ambiguity while preserving logarithmic qubit scaling.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The encoding addresses an information bottleneck that downstream quantum circuits cannot fix, without adding trainable parameters.
method: Establish an architecture-independent restriction caused by normalization-induced scale invariance.
Derive a condition for deterministic preprocessing to remove ambiguity; nonlinearity alone is insufficient.
Construct a fixed nonlinear feature map that distinguishes all real inputs after amplitude encoding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three canonical classification benchmarks and one nonlinear synthetic dataset, the abstract reports 21–44% accuracy improvements over amplitude- and angle-encoding baselines, with a classical neural network also evaluated.
infographic.watch_item: Logarithmic qubit scaling does not establish efficient state preparation; practical encoding costs and hardware performance remain unspecified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Overcoming the Representational Limitations of Amplitude Encoding for Quantum Neural Networks

title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks
authors: Javaria Ghafoor, Amr Sabry
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms leave the durations of Hamiltonian evolutions open for a classical optimizer to set. We present VHamilton, a minimal extension of the Hamilton quantum programming language in which such durations are open clocks: one program denotes a family of Hamiltonian trajectories, and a valuation fills its clocks with exact dyadic times, so that each instance is an ordinary Hamilton program that compiles to circuits as before. Because the semantics stays exact and affine in the clocks, the Hamiltonian structure of a variational program remainsavail able for reasoning about every valuation at once. Equivalence becomes a finite calculation, which we mechanize in Agda for a fragment and use to prove the VHamilton form of the compiler rewrite "rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx" for every clock value. We then show what the same structure supports in a two-qubit chemistry eigensolver written in VHamilton and run through a Haskell prototype. It supports a fusion of commuting blocks, a closed form and an expressibility proof for the ansatz, and an exact split of the error between the precision of the target and that of the clocks, with a priori bounds. It also supports a coordinate search whose queries per sweep, fixed by the spectra of the generators, do not grow with the precision. On the benchmark this search reaches the numerically verified optimum of a grid of 134 million valuations in 53 energy queries. It finds the grid optimum in only 21 of 30 validation settings, however, so the gain is conditional, not a global-optimization guarantee.

infographic.key_insight: VHamilton represents variational evolution times as open clocks, enabling exact reasoning and compiler equivalence proofs across all clock valuations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Preserving Hamiltonian structure supports verified circuit rewrites, commuting-block fusion, precision-error bounds, and spectrum-informed parameter search.
method: Instantiate open clocks with exact dyadic times to obtain ordinary Hamilton programs that compile to circuits.
Mechanize finite equivalence checks in Agda for a fragment, proving rzz(t) = cx; rz(t); cx for every clock value.

infographic.paper_title: Variational Programs with Open Clocks

title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization
authors: Filipe Chagas Ferraz
abstract: This article presents a predictive-maintenance pipeline that detects anomalies in bearings from vibration signals, adapted for deployment at the edge on low-cost microcontrollers, and that uses quantum optimization in two steps of its training. The pipeline consists of a step of vibration feature extraction and a step of classification with a one-class support vector machine (OCSVM). The features are selected by minimum redundancy and maximum relevance (mRMR) with the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE), under a limit on computing time. The OCSVM is adapted for inference at the edge without floating-point operations and is trained by a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE). In small-scale tests on a simulator, with the Paderborn bearing dataset, the VQE found the optimal selection in 36% of the runs with Adam, and PCE chose better support vectors than chance, until a classical local search made the two equal. A classical baseline, the usual OCSVM trained by SMO with its weights rounded, matched them without any search.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum-assisted training enabled a bearing-anomaly detection pipeline designed for microcontrollers, but showed no advantage over a rounded-weight classical OCSVM baseline.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline targets low-cost edge predictive maintenance with vibration features and OCSVM inference that avoids floating-point operations.
method: Extract vibration features and select them using mRMR optimized by VQE under a computing-time limit.
Train an OCSVM using a variational quantum algorithm with Pauli-correlation encoding (PCE).
Adapt OCSVM inference for microcontrollers without floating-point operations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Small-scale simulator tests on the Paderborn bearing dataset found optimal VQE selections in 36% of Adam runs; PCE beat chance before classical local search, while rounded-weight SMO matched performance without search.
infographic.watch_item: Simulator-only, small-scale results do not establish a quantum advantage or validate performance on physical quantum hardware and deployed microcontrollers.
infographic.paper_title: Predictive Maintenance at the Edge: An Embedded Anomaly Detection Pipeline Trained with Quantum Optimization

title: Quantum machine learning geospatial time-series by seasonal encoding
authors: Devjyoti Tripathy, Reece Robertson, Josey Stevens, Catherine Nakalembe, Sebastian Deffner
abstract: Quantum data reuploading models can increase the expressive capacity of variational quantum models, but do not necessarily improve predictive performance. In the present work, we investigate this behavior for seasonal time series forecasting and show that data encoding determines how well temporal structures are represented as circuit depth increases. We develop a fidelity-based quantum geometric description in which repeated encodings contribute to an effective input generator, so that reuploading depth changes the quantum geometry through which approximately recurrent inputs are distinguished. We construct fixed and adaptive seasonal encodings that represent observation magnitude and seasonal phase in distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates. We evaluate these encodings for monthly precipitation derived from ERA5-Land, a global reanalysis dataset, from a representative semi-arid, drought-prone tropical region in East Africa, using a 14-month lag window and reuploading depths $L$= 1-6. We find that in ideal simulations, standard value-based encodings degrade markedly with depth, whereas adaptive seasonal encodings preserve temporal correlation, spectral structure, and forecasting accuracy. Noisy simulations show that this encoding hierarchy persists at shallow and intermediate depths, while larger depths are limited by circuit noise and optimization difficulty. The seasonal quantum models remain competitive with established classical forecasting methods (ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs). These results identify structure-aware quantum data encoding as a general strategy for building deeper quantum reuploading models.

infographic.key_insight: Encoding seasonal structure helps quantum data-reuploading models retain forecasting accuracy as circuit depth increases, while standard value-based encodings degrade.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-aware encoding offers a practical design strategy for deeper quantum time-series models, though circuit noise and optimization remain constraints.
method: Use fidelity-based quantum geometry to analyze how repeated encodings distinguish recurrent inputs.
Encode observation magnitude and seasonal phase in distinct Bloch-sphere coordinates using fixed or adaptive schemes.
Evaluate 14-month lag forecasts across reuploading depths L = 1–6.
infographic.evidence_signal: On monthly ERA5-Land precipitation from a semi-arid East African region, adaptive seasonal encodings preserved temporal and spectral structure in ideal simulations; seasonal models remained competitive with ARIMA, random forests, and LSTMs.
infographic.watch_item: Noisy simulations limited deeper circuits, and evaluation in one representative region does not establish broad generalization or quantum advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum machine learning geospatial time-series by seasonal encoding

title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction
authors: Yuguo Shao, Zhenyu Chen, Ningfeng Wang, Song Cheng, Zhaohui Wei, Zi-Wen Liu
abstract: We introduce FaultScope, a classical simulator for quantum error correction circuits, implemented in Rust with a Python interface. FaultScope estimates logical error rates and their derivatives with respect to component error rates from the same sampled and decoded shots, without modifying or differentiating through the decoder. These derivatives enable error attribution to individual noisy components, helping identify noise hotspots for targeted noise reduction. FaultScope supports forward simulation of error propagation through circuits and direct sampling of detector and logical observable outcomes from detector error models. In our noiseless and noisy benchmarks, FaultScope has the lowest runtime among the tested simulators at every size. Computing all derivatives adds only 0.33--0.97\% to the runtime of logical error rate estimation across five repetition code sizes with 7--2047 error locations. FaultScope can be used to benchmark large-scale quantum error correction schemes and guide targeted noise reduction efficiently, thereby facilitating the design and optimization of fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.

infographic.key_insight: FaultScope estimates logical error rates and attributes their sensitivity to individual noisy components using the same sampled and decoded shots.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can identify noise hotspots and prioritize component improvements when optimizing fault-tolerant quantum computing architectures.
method: Rust simulator with a Python interface for quantum error correction circuits.

infographic.paper_title: FaultScope: A software package for fast error attribution in quantum error correction

title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors
authors: Esteban Payares, Nadia Milazzo, Ghada Ben Slama, Thomas Cope
abstract: Despite quantum machine learning being an active topic of research, demonstrations of algorithms run on quantum hardware beating classical methods remain rare. In this work, we demonstrate a significant performance gap using a projected quantum kernel for $n=15,30$ and $45$ qubits over classical methods on an engineered classification problem, and show reproducibility of the results over different quantum processor units. We also demonstrate how error mitigation can widen this gap, both by improving hardware performance but also by increasing the classical difficulty, with different techniques contributing unequally to these phenomena. This work provides strong evidence that superior empirical performance of quantum hardware over all classical techniques is an achievable goal in quantum machine learning, albeit for an artificial problem. However, as with any application relying on observables, beating state-of-the-art simulation methods remains the primary challenge, as our matrix product state results here show.

infographic.key_insight: Projected quantum kernels on noisy processors outperformed tested classical methods on an engineered classification task, but state-of-the-art simulation remains a key challenge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results motivate reproducible quantum-learning benchmarks that assess error mitigation alongside strong classical simulators.
method: Use projected quantum kernels for engineered classification problems.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a significant performance gap at all three qubit counts, reproducibility across processors, and mitigation-dependent gains in hardware performance and classical difficulty.

infographic.paper_title: Engineered Learning Problems on Noisy Quantum Processors

title: Quantum Bernstein--Kolmogorov--Arnold approximation
authors: Sviatoslav V. Dzhenzher
abstract: This paper addresses the expressivity and representation gap in Quantum Neural Networks by establishing a quantum analogue of the classical Kolmogorov--Arnold representation theorem. We propose a constructive approximation framework over fixed input coherent states, where the dependence of the function argument is embedded entirely in coordinate qubits, while the target function dictates a single outer unitary evolution. By applying a Sprecher-type representation to the rotation angle of the state, we demonstrate that the multidimensional operator factorises into \(2d+1\) commuting universal inner observables. We prove that the resulting measurement probability precisely reproduces the multidimensional Bernstein polynomial of the target function. For any continuous multivariate function, the joint quantum state converges uniformly to the target output register, linking classical superposition theory with probabilistic and coherent quantum circuits.

infographic.key_insight: A constructive quantum analogue of Kolmogorov–Arnold representation reproduces multivariate Bernstein polynomials as measurement probabilities and establishes uniform convergence for continuous target functions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a principled route to expressive quantum function approximation, separating input encoding in coordinate qubits from a target-dependent outer unitary.
method: Encode function arguments in fixed input coherent states using coordinate qubits.
Apply a Sprecher-type representation to the state’s rotation angle, yielding 2d+1 commuting universal inner observables.

infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical proofs of exact Bernstein-polynomial reproduction and uniform convergence, but no numerical benchmarks or hardware experiments.
infographic.watch_item: Practical feasibility depends on the resource and synthesis costs of input preparation and the target-dependent unitary, which the abstract does not quantify.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Bernstein--Kolmogorov--Arnold approximation

title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation
authors: Yu-Ting Kao, Yeong-Jar Chang
abstract: This paper proposes a VLSI-like design and verification flow for quantum circuit implementation, covering four levels: behavioral modeling, register-transfer level (RTL), gate level, and full-circuit integration with quantum algorithms. Using quantum Monte Carlo methods for pi estimation as a case study, the proposed flow provides a systematic path from initial specifications to large-scale quantum circuit implementation. The paper highlights two key contributions. First, quantum digital design supports a broad range of applications beyond predefined circuit templates. This capability is particularly important for application-specific operations in algorithms such as Shor's, Grover's, and quantum amplitude estimation (QAE), and can significantly advance fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC). Second, classical simulation shows that replacing random sampling with grid sampling can achieve a quadratic improvement in this pi-estimation case without quantum computation. This suggests that the quadratic speedup may arise from the grid sampling strategy rather than from the QAE circuit itself. By adapting conventional VLSI digital design principles, this four-level flow addresses a key bottleneck in quantum circuit design and enables flexible design initiation from multiple entry points, including specifications, RTL, and gate-level descriptions, paving the way for the practical deployment of quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: A four-level, VLSI-like workflow structures quantum circuit design, while a pi-estimation case study suggests the observed quadratic improvement may stem from grid sampling rather than QAE itself.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports application-specific quantum operations and design entry at specification, RTL, or gate level, offering a systematic route toward larger quantum implementations.
method: Progress through behavioral modeling, RTL, gate-level design, and full-circuit integration.
Apply the workflow to quantum Monte Carlo pi estimation.

infographic.watch_item: The sampling result is case-specific, and the abstract does not establish hardware scalability or fault-tolerant resource costs.
infographic.paper_title: A VLSI-Like Design and Verification Flow for Quantum Circuits: A Case Study in PI Estimation

title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference
authors: George Kourousias, Sergio Carrato, Roberto Pugliese, Panagiotis Dimitrakis, Alberto Carini
abstract: An algebraic correspondence between an imaging model and a quantum state does not specify a computational method: input access, measurement and decoding determine what can be returned. This exposition develops four distinctions for computational-imaging and engineering readers. It separates amplitude encodings of input values from encodings of complete candidate labelings, explaining why amplitude storage does not provide full-array readout. Complex-field interference motivates unknown-phase inference: complementary measurements resolve ambiguities that local Fisher information alone does not detect. Reshaping joint amplitudes into a matrix connects singular-value decomposition to pure-state entanglement, while distinguishing Schmidt rank from conditions for efficient classical simulation. In a four-pixel segmentation, an objective becomes a cost operator and a sampling circuit. One layer of the quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) lowers mean energy from $1.675$ to $0.686$ relative to uniform sampling, yet makes a nonoptimal labeling more probable than the optimum 0.484 versus 0.365. Archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable local boundary decision. Low-rank state reconstruction and selected quantum algorithms connect these distinctions to an end-to-end resource account. The derivations and reproducible numerical references assume complex linear algebra and probability, without prior quantum mechanics. The accompanying Seeing Amplitudes browser laboratory supports interactive exploration; the article remains self-contained and connects each representation to the estimate or decision it permits and the resources that output requires.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum representations become useful computational methods only when input access, measurement, and decoding deliver the required estimate or decision.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For imaging workflows, evaluate quantum approaches by end-to-end output quality and resource costs, not compact state representations alone.
method: Distinguish input-amplitude encodings from candidate-labeling encodings and their readout limits.
Use complementary measurements for phase inference and matrix SVD to explain pure-state entanglement.
Map four-pixel segmentation to a cost operator and a one-layer QAOA sampling circuit.
infographic.evidence_signal: In four-pixel segmentation, one QAOA layer reduced mean energy from 1.675 to 0.686 versus uniform sampling, but a nonoptimal labeling remained more probable than the optimum (0.484 versus 0.365); archived IBM and IQM measurements illustrate a separate six-variable boundary decision.
infographic.watch_item: Lower mean energy does not guarantee the most likely optimal solution, and amplitude storage does not provide full-array readout.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Computing through Computational Imaging: Representations, Measurement, and Inference

title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels
authors: Keitaro Anai, Akimoto Nakayama, Shintaro Ooka, Hiroko Tomoda, Yuto Morohoshi, Yohji Chin
abstract: Analyzing quantum systems is essential for quantum information processing, but can require exponentially many measurements without exploiting the structure of the system or task. Quantum machine learning offers a promising way to reduce this cost by learning from quantum data. Here, we theoretically establish a framework for efficient quantum-state classification and experimentally demonstrate the resulting scheme on a programmable photonic processor. Our analysis links learning efficiency to the structure of quantum data, without relying on a physical description tailored to each task. We derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with a number of measurements polynomial in system size. We apply this guarantee to a resource problem in continuous-variable (CV) quantum computing: classifying stellar rank, a measure of non-Gaussianity. Experimentally, we implement the classification of single-mode CV quantum states with stellar rank zero and one. This is enabled by developing a programmable CV photonic processor capable of preparing and processing diverse Gaussian and non-Gaussian states and performing virtual projection onto such states, going beyond the Gaussian-only capabilities of most existing photonic platforms. The experiment demonstrates accurate classification despite experimental imperfections. Our results establish a theory-guided and experimentally validated framework for quantum-state classification that can be implemented on quantum devices available today.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum kernels enable efficient quantum-state classification under sufficient structural conditions, with measurement requirements polynomial in system size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A programmable photonic processor extends beyond Gaussian-only operations to prepare, process, and virtually project onto Gaussian and non-Gaussian states.
method: Link classification efficiency to quantum-data structure.
Derive sufficient conditions for accurate classification with polynomially many measurements.
Classify single-mode states of stellar rank zero versus one using a programmable photonic processor.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports accurate experimental classification despite imperfections, but provides no numerical accuracy or measurement counts.
infographic.watch_item: The efficiency guarantee is conditional, and the experimental demonstration is limited to single-mode states with stellar rank zero or one.
infographic.paper_title: Provably efficient experimental classification of quantum data with quantum kernels

title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU
authors: R. Pradeep, Anurag Chaudhary, Ashish Kumar Patra, Anurag K. S. V., Ruchika Bhat, Sai Shankar P.
abstract: Present-day sample-based quantum algorithms within quantum-centric supercomputing workflows require substantial classical post-processing, large circuit depths to produce chemically relevant samples, and long QPU times to execute the many circuits needed for molecules of chemically relevant size. We introduce FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD, a resource-efficient sample-based framework that breaks a large problem into fragments, runs the fragments in parallel on virtual regions of the QPU, and reduces circuit depth through a half-qubit ansatz whose samples seed an HCI expansion. We demonstrate the algorithm on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston for the water trimer and the carmofur_Mpro complex with up to 52 qubits, benchmarking against FMO-CCSD(T), FMO-CASCI and FMO-HCI. For the water trimer (14 spin orbitals for monomers, 28 for dimers), our method reduces the two-qubit depth by 39% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD and the QPU time by 82% compared to sequential FMO-SQD, and accesses 3% of the determinant subspace versus 40% for FMO-SQD, while achieving more accurate energies. For the carmofur_Mpro complex (16 and 32 spin orbitals), it reduces the two-qubit depth by 47% and the QPU time by 20% compared to FMO-QVM-SQD, and accesses 0.007% of the determinant subspace versus 40%, while remaining within chemical accuracy. Extending the carmofur_Mpro active space in the 6-31G basis to 52 and 104 spin orbitals, sampled on 26 and 52 qubits, the total energy deviates from FMO-HCI by only 1.22 mHa. These results show that combining fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling makes sample-based quantum simulation of chemically relevant systems feasible on current hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Combining molecular fragmentation, virtual QPU partitioning and half-qubit sampling reduces quantum simulation resources while preserving accurate molecular energies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework enables parallel fragment execution and shallower circuits on current QPUs, reducing runtime and classical determinant-space demands.
method: Split molecular calculations into fragments using FMO.
Execute fragment circuits in parallel on virtual QPU regions.
Seed HCI expansion with half-qubit ansatz samples in FMO-QVM-HCI-HSQD.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on ibm_marrakesh and ibm_boston showed 39% lower two-qubit depth versus FMO-QVM-SQD and 82% less QPU time versus sequential FMO-SQD for the water trimer; the largest carmofur_Mpro calculation used 52 qubits and differed from FMO-HCI by 1.22 mHa.
infographic.watch_item: Resource savings depend on the system and comparison baseline; broader scalability beyond the demonstrated molecules and 52-qubit execution remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Resource efficient Sample Based Quantum Simulation through Fragmentation and Virtual Partitioning of QPU

title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory
authors: Tairong Bai, Wen Zheng, Haoyang Cai, Xianke Li, Yangyang Ge, Kun Zhou
abstract: In continuous-variable quantum information, sensing and quantum error correction in the same mode face an intrinsic trade-off: sensors must accumulate weak external displacements, whereas bosonic codes typically suppress such shifts as errors. Here, we establish compatibility by constructing finite-energy bosonic codes that enable a single oscillator to sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit. By encoding logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites and capturing the force signal in a shared internal coordinate, we achieve an endpoint probe readout that is independent of the logical state under continuous photon loss $γ$. Crucially, binomial site recovery cancels packet-dependent probe distortions alongside logical errors: for a $(2r+2)$-packet code, memory infidelity is suppressed to $O(γ^{r+1})$ while residual memory-probe correlations scale as $O(γ^{r+2})$. Finally, superconducting quantum circuit benchmarks under competing photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity identify preferred encoding regimes for hardware implementation.

infographic.key_insight: Finite-energy bosonic codes let one oscillator sense an external force while actively protecting an unknown logical qubit, with probe readout independent of the logical state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could combine force sensing and recoverable quantum memory in superconducting hardware without assigning them separate oscillator modes.
method: Encode logical amplitudes across discrete wave-packet sites.
Capture the force signal in a shared internal coordinate.
Use binomial site recovery to correct logical errors and packet-dependent probe distortions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports memory infidelity scaling as O(γ^(r+1)) and residual memory–probe correlations as O(γ^(r+2)) for a (2r+2)-packet code under photon loss γ, plus superconducting-circuit benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Photon-number dephasing and Kerr nonlinearity compete with photon-loss protection, making encoding choice hardware-dependent.
infographic.paper_title: Force Sensing in a Recoverable Bosonic Quantum Memory

title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing
authors: Anna Brünisholz, Markus Reiher
abstract: Future fault-tolerant quantum computers will allow us to calculate electronic structures of atomistic systems. However, these systems will be intrinsically limited in size, requiring embedding theories for many systems because of the unfavorable scaling of the number of terms describing the electron-electron interaction in the second-quantized electronic Hamiltonian. Quantum embedding theories address this challenge by partitioning a quantum system into a region of interest, the impurity, and its (larger) complement, the environment. However, currently available quantum embedding methods place restrictive demands on near-future quantum computers, such as the need to measure reduced density matrices or the need for repeated evaluations. Here, we introduce the new orbital embedding method eCAS that steers clear of these pitfalls by constructing a multi-CAS problem, the active spaces of which are localized and can be solved independently of each other with any quantum algorithm. This also allows for the development of comparatively simple gradient expressions. eCAS leverages the Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals and augments them with localized environment orbitals, based on a mutual correlation criterion. The mutual correlation criterion makes eCAS systematically improvable without the need for any iteratively determined quantities.

infographic.key_insight: eCAS partitions electronic-structure calculations into localized active spaces that can be solved independently with quantum algorithms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets size-limited quantum computers while avoiding reduced-density-matrix measurements and repeated evaluations required by some embedding approaches.
method: Use Schmidt decomposition to construct initial impurity and bath orbitals.
Add localized environment orbitals using a mutual correlation criterion.
Solve the resulting multiple complete active spaces independently, with systematic refinement and comparatively simple gradients.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the method and its systematic improvability but reports no numerical benchmarks or hardware demonstrations.
infographic.watch_item: Practical accuracy and quantum-resource savings need benchmarking as active spaces are enlarged.
infographic.paper_title: eCAS: An Orbital Embedding Method for Quantum Computing

title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels
authors: Ronak Bhalgami
abstract: Quantum kernel methods are the most concrete near-term proposal for quantum machine learning on classical data, yet published benchmarks disagree on whether they outperform tuned classical kernels, and the disagreement cannot be resolved from the literature because the comparisons are not protocol-controlled. We argue that the obstacle is one of measurement, not theory: the usual setup fixes the quantum feature map's data scaling while grid-searching the classical kernel's hyperparameters, recomputes nothing per fold, and reports cost in simulator time. We therefore treat the comparison itself as the object of study and impose three controls. The bandwidth is tuned on the same grid budget as the classical $γ$, the kernel is recomputed inside every fold from fold-fitted preprocessing, and cost is counted in hardware circuit evaluations. On top of these we run a factorial design of 324 cells in which dimensionality, training size, class separability and data structure are explicit covariates, together with four standard datasets, a shots-versus-gate-noise ablation, and a cost sweep. The dominant effect we measure is not quantum: tuning the feature map's bandwidth is worth 0.120 accuracy on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data, exceeding every quantum-classical difference we observe. Tuned quantum kernels are then statistically indistinguishable from a tuned RBF on all four real datasets. The advantage on synthetic data is confined almost entirely to data generated by the feature map itself, and it shrinks with dimensionality (-0.0045 per qubit) while growing with sample size. Finite sampling costs an order of magnitude more accuracy than gate and readout noise, and a fidelity kernel needs $5\times10^{7}$ circuits at n = 10,000. Protocol variance is thus sufficient to explain the field's contradictory conclusions.

infographic.key_insight: Fair bandwidth tuning matters more than the observed quantum–classical accuracy differences, with tuned quantum kernels statistically indistinguishable from tuned RBF kernels on four real datasets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantum-kernel evaluations should use matched tuning budgets, fold-specific preprocessing and kernel recomputation, and hardware circuit counts rather than simulator runtime.
method: Match quantum bandwidth and classical kernel tuning budgets.
Refit preprocessing and recompute kernels within every fold.
Evaluate 324 factorial-design cells, four real datasets, noise ablations, and a circuit-cost sweep.
infographic.evidence_signal: Bandwidth tuning improved accuracy by 0.120 on synthetic data and 0.339 on real data; synthetic quantum advantages occurred almost entirely on data generated by the feature map itself.
infographic.watch_item: Hardware scaling remains a concern: a fidelity kernel requires about 50 million circuit evaluations at 10,000 samples, and finite-shot sampling degraded accuracy more than gate and readout noise.
infographic.paper_title: Empirical Evaluation of Quantum Kernel Methods for Classification: A Comparative Study with Classical Kernels

title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
authors: Tianhao Guo, Dianxin Zheng, Yuhua Qian, Yaohui Zheng, Yuzhi Yang, Merouane Debbah
abstract: In quantum computing, the readout always carries finite-shot sampling noise. Suppressing this noise through repeated measurements raises the cost of a quantum neural network (QNN). Meanwhile, a stochastic diffusion sampler deliberately adds randomness at each reverse (generation) step. This paper turns the measurement noise from a liability into a resource. Specifically, we use the noise quantum measurement produces anyway to replace part of the noise the sampler would otherwise inject. We characterize the measurement error as multinomial sampling noise propagated through a trainable linear readout. To connect the circuit's Born probabilities to the denoising task, we further formulate the diffusion process on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex. Therefore, we can employ a compensation noise to match the mean and covariance of the shot-noise-free linear update under some minimum shot conditions. Solving this condition for the shot count gives a state-dependent adaptive budget. For the denoising diffusion implicit model (DDIM), this budget increases as the sampler becomes more deterministic. On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the schedule achieves comparable generation quality with $303$ shots per sample against a high-shot reference of $1.6\times10^{6}$, about $5300\times$ fewer. Latent diffusion experiments on MNIST further validate the proposed mechanism for generation in a learned latent space.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum measurement noise can replace part of the randomness required by diffusion sampling, reducing measurement shots rather than merely suppressing noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: State-dependent shot budgets offer a route to lower quantum sampling costs while preserving diffusion generation quality.
method: Model finite-shot readout error as multinomial noise propagated through a trainable linear readout.
Formulate diffusion on a bounded zero-sum hyperplane mapped to the probability simplex.
Add compensation noise to match the ideal linear update’s mean and covariance, deriving an adaptive minimum shot budget.
infographic.evidence_signal: On an eight-dimensional Gaussian mixture, the method achieved comparable generation quality using 303 shots per sample versus a 1.6-million-shot reference—about 5,300× fewer—with additional validation on MNIST latent diffusion.
infographic.watch_item: Moment matching requires minimum shot conditions, and the DDIM shot budget rises as sampling becomes more deterministic.
infographic.paper_title: Leveraging Quantum Measurement Randomness for Shot-Efficient Diffusion Models
